config.title: Conditional Classes

intro.title: Conditional Classes
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular component that toggles the visual style of a button based on user interaction. You will learn how to apply CSS classes conditionally using Angular's built-in directive for dynamic styling. The core concept involves binding class names to component properties that change in response to events. You'll work with TypeScript for logic, Angular templates for structure, and CSS for styling to create an interactive UI element.
intro.usecase: Conditional classes are essential for creating responsive, interactive interfaces in real-world Angular applications. In dashboard applications, they're used to highlight active menu items or indicate status changes like turning a metric card red when values exceed thresholds. Form validations frequently apply conditional classes to show error states on input fields with red borders when validation fails. E-commerce sites use them to toggle product filters or indicate selected items in shopping carts with visual feedback. This pattern creates intuitive user experiences by providing immediate visual cues based on application state.

objectives: Apply the ngClass directive to conditionally set CSS classes based on component state.
Construct a component property to control the boolean condition for class application.
Bind an HTML element's class to a component method that returns a class string dynamically.
Configure ngClass with an object syntax to toggle multiple classes based on different conditions.
Integrate user interactions, such as button clicks, to manipulate the conditional class state.
Initialize a component with default state values that determine the initial class rendering.

steps.title: Import Component and CommonModule
steps.instruction: Import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common' to set up your Angular component.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in these Angular core dependencies.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the necessary imports to create an Angular component with template directives.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core' and CommonModule is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.

steps.title: Create the main component class
steps.instruction: Create a component class named ConditionalClassesComponent with the @Component decorator and selector 'app-conditional-classes'.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator from '@angular/core' to define your component. The selector should match the HTML tag you'll use in templates.
steps.expectedOutcome: A component class is defined with the correct name and decorator configuration.
successCriteria: ConditionalClassesComponent class exists with @Component decorator having selector 'app-conditional-classes'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the class name is exactly 'ConditionalClassesComponent' and the selector is set to 'app-conditional-classes' in the @Component decorator.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class wasn't created correctly. Check that you used the @Component decorator with the proper selector and exported the class.

steps.title: Add component metadata and template
steps.instruction: Add the @Component decorator to your ConditionalClassesComponent class with template and styles properties. Set template to an empty string and styles to an empty array.
steps.hint: Use @Component({ template: '', styles: [] }) above your class declaration.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have metadata configured with empty template and styles.
successCriteria: Component decorator is added with template and styles properties set as empty.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added both template and styles properties to the @Component decorator.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component decorator is missing or incomplete. Check that you've added template and styles properties.

steps.title: Initialize a boolean state property
steps.instruction: In your ConditionalClassesComponent class, add a boolean property named 'isActive' and initialize it to false.
steps.hint: Add a property declaration inside the class body, like 'isActive = false;'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have a boolean property 'isActive' set to false, which will later control conditional class application.
successCriteria: The ConditionalClassesComponent class contains a property 'isActive' initialized to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a property, but check that it's named exactly 'isActive' and initialized to false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The property 'isActive' is missing or not correctly initialized to false. Review the instruction.

steps.title: Create a toggle handler method
steps.instruction: Inside the ConditionalClassesComponent class, add a method named toggleActive that toggles the isActive property between true and false.
steps.hint: You can toggle a boolean by setting it to the opposite of its current value using the logical NOT operator (!).
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a toggleActive method that can be called to change the isActive state.
successCriteria: A toggleActive method is defined in the ConditionalClassesComponent class that toggles the isActive property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but make sure it's named toggleActive and correctly toggles the isActive property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleActive method is not properly defined. Check that it's inside the class and correctly toggles the isActive property.

steps.title: Add a div with conditional class binding
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add a <div> element with a conditional class binding that applies the 'active' CSS class when the isActive property is true. Use Angular's [class.className] syntax.
steps.hint: The syntax is [class.active]="isActive". This will add the 'active' class to the div when isActive is true, and remove it when false.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will contain a div element with conditional class binding that responds to the isActive property.
successCriteria: The template includes a <div> element with [class.active] binding to the isActive property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a div element, but it's missing the conditional class binding. Make sure to use [class.active]="isActive" to bind the class to the property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't contain the required conditional class binding. Add a <div> element with [class.active]="isActive" to apply the 'active' class conditionally.

steps.title: Add CSS styles for the active class
steps.instruction: In the component's styles array, add a CSS rule for the .active class that sets background-color to 'lightblue' and color to 'darkblue'.
steps.hint: Add a styles property to the @Component decorator with an array containing a CSS rule for .active.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a styles array with a CSS rule for .active that changes the visual appearance when applied.
successCriteria: The @Component decorator includes a styles property with an array containing '.active { background-color: lightblue; color: darkblue; }'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your CSS rule includes both background-color and color properties with the specified values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for .active is missing or incorrect. Make sure to add a styles array to the @Component decorator with the correct CSS rule.

steps.title: Add a button to trigger state change
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add a button element with a click event bound to the toggleActive() method. The button should have the text 'Toggle Active'.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (click)="handler()" to connect the button click to your toggle method.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button with click handler
<button (click)="handleClick()">Click Me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Toggle Active' appears in the component's template, which when clicked will toggle the isActive state.
successCriteria: The template contains a button element with (click)="toggleActive()" event binding and the text 'Toggle Active'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the button has both the click event binding and the correct text label.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured. Check that you're using Angular's (click) syntax and calling toggleActive().

steps.title: Add text content to demonstrate state
steps.instruction: Inside the component's template, add a paragraph element that displays the current value of the isActive property using interpolation.
steps.hint: Use double curly braces {{ }} to interpolate the isActive property value in the template.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a boolean value in template

Current state: {{ isActive }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will show a paragraph that displays 'false' initially and updates to 'true' when the button is clicked.
successCriteria: A paragraph element with interpolation {{ isActive }} is added to the component template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a paragraph, but make sure it uses interpolation {{ isActive }} to display the property value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element with interpolation {{ isActive }} is missing or incorrect.

steps.title: Test the conditional class behavior
steps.instruction: Run the application and click the button to verify that the conditional class is being applied and removed correctly when the button is clicked.
steps.hint: Start your development server, open the app in your browser, and click the button to see the visual changes.
steps.analogousExample:
// Testing conditional behavior
// After running the app, click the button to see the class toggle.
steps.expectedOutcome: The application runs successfully, and clicking the button toggles the visual appearance of the component by applying/removing the conditional class.
successCriteria: The app runs without errors, and clicking the button visibly toggles the component's styling.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: The app runs, but the conditional class might not be visibly toggling. Check that your button click handler is properly wired and the CSS styles are applied.
steps.feedbackWrong: The app doesn't run or the conditional class doesn't toggle. Verify your component setup, button binding, and CSS styles.
